intros.market: Five CAs control 88.8% of all publicly trusted issuance, with Internet Security Research Group leading at 32.6%, followed by Google Trust Services at 21.0% and DigiCert at 17.8%. The three-firm concentration ratio stands at 71.4%, while 74 CAs collectively issue the remaining 11.2% of certificates. This concentration creates systemic dependency on a handful of operators, amplifying the impact of any single CA failure or distrust event.
intros.trust: 335 roots are distributed across the four major trust stores, but only 90 roots appear in all four stores and just 38 CA owners maintain universal presence. Microsoft carries 142 roots not trusted by Chrome, Mozilla, or Apple, creating deployment complexity where certificate chains valid in Edge may fail in other browsers. Store disagreement forces CAs to maintain multiple hierarchies and complicates incident response when only a subset of root programs takes enforcement action.
intros.conc: The market HHI of 2015 indicates moderate concentration approaching the 2500 threshold where systemic risk accelerates. The top three CAs alone issue 71.4% of all certificates, creating single points of failure where operational issues or compliance failures at ISRG, Google, or DigiCert could disrupt trust for the majority of the web. This concentration intersects with geographic risk, as all three dominant players are incorporated in the United States.
intros.tail: 74 CAs operate outside the top five, collectively issuing just 11.2% of certificates yet maintaining full trust store inclusion with identical browser impact as high-volume operators. Each tail CA represents independent operational risk with limited ecosystem visibility and oversight resources spread thin across 88 trusted entities. The long tail contributes disproportionately to governance complexity while serving minimal issuance volume.
intros.geo: CAs incorporated in the United States issue 92.75% of all certificates, with Europe at 7.16% and Asia-Pacific at 0.09%, creating extreme geographic concentration beyond market share alone. 15 US-based CAs dominate the global trust infrastructure, while 44 European CAs and 17 Asia-Pacific CAs collectively serve less than 8% of issuance. This concentration amplifies jurisdiction risk, as US legal frameworks and government demands affect the vast majority of certificate issuance worldwide.
intros.gov: 30 government-operated or state-owned CAs hold positions in public trust stores, collectively issuing 0.09% of certificates. These entities operate under conflicting incentives where state intelligence and law enforcement priorities may supersede commercial security practices. Government CA presence creates compelled access risk regardless of issuance volume, as trust store inclusion grants capability to issue valid certificates for any domain.
intros.jurisdiction: Five jurisdictions are classified as high risk for compelled disclosure or lawful intercept mandates: China, Russia, the United Kingdom, Australia, and Hong Kong. India and Turkey present moderate risk under frameworks that permit government access to cryptographic systems. These legal frameworks intersect with geographic concentration, as the 92.75% US issuance share places most certificate infrastructure under FISA and national security letter authority.
intros.ops: 1,669 recorded incidents across 55 CAs break down as 642 misissuances, 538 governance failures, 359 revocation issues, and 130 validation errors. Only 29% of incidents are self-detected by the issuing CA, while 16% come from automated tools and 18% from external researchers, indicating persistent surveillance gaps in CA operations. 209 incidents involved policy failures and 154 involved disclosure failures, with just 8% of problems found through the formal audit process.
intros.crypto: Root algorithm distribution and key size compliance define the cryptographic baseline for trust anchors embedded in operating systems and browsers. Migration from SHA-1 to SHA-2 signatures and RSA key size requirements reflect evolving threat models, though legacy roots remain in stores years after algorithm deprecation. Cryptographic posture intersects with governance as root programs set standards but enforcement varies across Chrome, Mozilla, Apple, and Microsoft.
intros.distrust: 16 total distrust events have occurred across the ecosystem, with 14 attributed to compliance or operational failures and 10 following a pattern of repeated issues. The posture distribution shows 7 cases of negligent noncompliance, 3 of demonstrated incompetence, and 3 of willful circumvention, while the median runway from announcement to removal is 1,185 days. This extended timeline limits deterrent effect and allows problematic CAs to continue issuance during lengthy transition periods.
intros.policy: Of the 43 active TLS-issuing CAs measured, 5 remain at risk against the 100-day validity threshold effective March 2027, while only 8 demonstrate readiness for the 47-day limit planned for March 2029 with a current median issuance validity of 63 days. CAs must navigate a regulatory surface that has grown 121-fold since 2000, now encompassing 6,657 total obligations of which 5,056 are mandatory requirements across CA/B Forum baseline requirements, four root program policies, WebTrust and ETSI audit criteria, and IETF standards. The expanding compliance burden complicates readiness as CAs must simultaneously shorten issuance cycles and absorb accelerating policy growth, with zero new ballots passed since 2022 despite mounting obligations.
intros.governance: Chrome provided substantive oversight on 18.4% of the 223 incidents reported in 2025, down from 67.8% coverage in 2019, while Mozilla coverage fell from 78.0% to 9.9% and Apple covered just 5.4%. Microsoft provided zero substantive oversight in both periods despite operating a trust store with 142 unique roots. Declining engagement from root programs intersects with operational risk, as the 71% of incidents receiving no root program response in 2025 suggests weakening enforcement of the formal compliance framework.
intros.community: 56 organizations hold CA/B Forum membership but only 21 contribute actively, leaving 35 members with zero participation in standards development. Stephen Davidson of Sectigo has proposed 36 ballots and endorsed 1, while Sectigo leads organizational ballot activity across the forum. Silent majority dynamics concentrate policy influence among a small set of CAs while the broader membership benefits from trust store inclusion without contributing to governance work.
intros.audit: Auditors detected just 31% of the 429 in-scope incidents that occurred during their examination periods, with 131 findings captured in audit letters while 298 incidents emerged later through Bugzilla disclosure. 41 CAs show high transparency gaps between clean audit opinions and subsequent incident reports, while 6 CAs received qualified opinions and 10 have adopted ETSI EN 319 403 v3.5. Self-reporting rates of 62.4% for WebTrust and 68.6% for ETSI indicate most findings still come from external discovery rather than CA disclosure, connecting to the 29% self-detection rate in operational incident data.
